items.prose: Stretching No. 10 XX Dufour Swiss bolting silk across the hexagonal cedar reel achieved a precise 129-micron sieve cutoff. The fine silk gauze separated velvety endosperm patent flour from coarse sharps and golden semolina flakes.

Centrifugal beaters spinning at 220 RPM flung a stray piece of calcified dough against the cylinder wall, ripping a four-inch gash through the No. 12XX silk. Un-sifted coarse bran flakes flooded the patent flour collection bin before operators could trip the bypass.

High humidity (75% RH) triggered an outbreak of *Acarus siro* flour mites across the wooden reel frames. Microscopic cast skins and silk webbing clogged over 40% of the 180-micron pores, reducing bolter throughput from 400 kg/hr to a trickle.

Subterranean winter air (18% RH) generated severe electrostatic charges as flour granules cascaded over dry silk cloth. Flour clung stubbornly to the charged silk; installing grounded copper tinsel wiper brushes dissipated the charge and cleared the sieve mesh.

A thrown lead counterweight on the central vertical crank shaft threw the suspended twelve-sieve plansifter stack into violent elliptic wobble. The harmonic shaking tore the stapled silk edges away from four internal pine sieve frames.

Calibrating upward air aspiration currents through an oscillating silk sieve deck lifted papery 'bee-wing' bran particles into the dust collector. Dense, pure vitreous endosperm chunks fell through the graded silk, producing pristine semolina for pasta production.

Replacing fragile natural multifilament silk with precision woven polyamide (nylon) monofilament screen tripled operating life. The smooth synthetic fibers resisted fungal decay, eliminated thread shifting, and tolerated high-pressure steam sanitization.

Passing coarse bran flakes through a high-velocity rotating brush duster lined with 40-mesh phosphor-bronze wire cloth scoured off adherent flour dust. The mechanical scouring recovered an extra 3.5% flour yield that would otherwise have been lost to animal feed.
